facts.statement: The study examined how exosomes released from the brain during infection with pseudorabies virus (PRV) affect the spread of the virus and damage to the blood-brain barrier.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Exosomes were collected from the brains of mice infected with PRV and compared with those from mice that received a placebo treatment.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The researchers used microscopy and protein analysis to verify that the collected samples contained exosomes and not whole virus particles.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Exosomes from infected mice carried viral genetic material and proteins, and they successfully passed the virus to pig kidney cells in the lab.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: In a laboratory model of the blood-brain barrier made of specific brain cell types, the exosomes caused the barrier to lose its protective function.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: When exosomes from infected mice were injected into the brains of living animals, the animals showed signs of nerve damage and their blood-brain barriers became more leaky.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The results suggest that exosomes from the brain are a previously overlooked way the virus spreads and causes injury to blood vessels in the nervous system.
facts.subject: animals
